It is best to deal with issues of around the death of others before a child actually experiences it first-hand.� Children can start understanding the topic around age three or four.� If young children are prepared for small deaths (like a pet), then they will be better prepared for more significant deaths they will face later, such as family members.

The emotional pain experienced by children around death include shock, anger, worry, perhaps guilt and sometimes feelings of abandonment.� They may not show grief through crying, but may show�aggression, withdrawal, moodiness, eating disruptions and sleeping disorders.� Young children may not verbally express their grief; instead they may show it through artwork, music or role playing.

Tips For helping Children Deal With Death
  • Be straightforward and don't use euphemisms like "they have gone to sleep".� Explain by, "When people are dead their bodies don't work anymore. When people die they are gone from our lives and do not come back."
  • Talk openly about the situation.� It is a normal part of our lives.
  • Mention that the dead go to a place that is safe and good, but stress that they should not ake steps to join the dead
  • Get the child to remember happy times withthe deceased.� Listen to their expressions of grief and reassure them it is okay to feel that grief.
  • Talk to the child about what can be done to help them through the process of mourning
